claims.evidence: Directly stated in the introduction and supported by citations to prior literature.

claims.claim: A large body of research has described differences in decision-related dynamics across brain areas.
claims.source: A large body of research has described differences in decision-related dynamics across brain areas (Ding and Gold, 2012; Thura and Cisek, 2014; Roitman and Shadlen, 2002; Hanks et al., 2015) and a smaller set of studies has provided insight into layer-dependent dynamics during decision-making (Chandrasekaran et al., 2017; Finn et al., 2019; Chandrasekaran et al., 2019; Bastos et al., 2018).
claims.evidence: Directly stated in the introduction and supported by citations to prior literature.

claims.claim: A smaller set of studies has provided insight into layer-dependent dynamics during decision-making.
claims.source: A large body of research has described differences in decision-related dynamics across brain areas (Ding and Gold, 2012; Thura and Cisek, 2014; Roitman and Shadlen, 2002; Hanks et al., 2015) and a smaller set of studies has provided insight into layer-dependent dynamics during decision-making (Chandrasekaran et al., 2017; Finn et al., 2019; Chandrasekaran et al., 2019; Bastos et al., 2018).
claims.evidence: Directly stated in the introduction and supported by citations to prior literature.

claims.claim: We currently do not understand how decision-related dynamics emerge across putative cell types.
claims.source: However, we currently do not understand how decision-related dynamics emerge across putative cell types.
claims.evidence: Directly stated in the introduction as a gap in knowledge.

claims.claim: In mice, and to some extent in rats, transgenic tools allow the in vivo detection of particular cell types.
claims.source: In mice, and to some extent in rats, transgenic tools allow the in vivo detection of particular cell types (Pinto and Dan, 2015; Lui et al., 2021), whereas in vivo studies in primates are largely restricted to using features of the extracellular action potential (EAP) such as trough to peak duration, spike width, and cell firing rate (FR).
claims.evidence: Directly stated in the introduction and supported by citations to prior literature.

claims.claim: In vivo studies in primates are largely restricted to using features of the extracellular action potential (EAP) such as trough to peak duration, spike width, and cell firing rate (FR).
claims.source: In mice, and to some extent in rats, transgenic tools allow the in vivo detection of particular cell types (Pinto and Dan, 2015; Lui et al., 2021), whereas in vivo studies in primates are largely restricted to using features of the extracellular action potential (EAP) such as trough to peak duration, spike width, and cell firing rate (FR).
claims.evidence: Directly stated in the introduction as a limitation of primate studies.

claims.claim: Early in vivo monkey work introduced the importance of EAP features, such as spike duration and action potential (AP) width, in identifying cell types.
claims.source: Early in vivo monkey work (Mountcastle et al., 1969) introduced the importance of EAP features, such as spike duration and action potential (AP) width, in identifying cell types.
claims.evidence: Directly stated in the introduction and supported by a citation to prior literature.

claims.claim: Early experiments introduced the concept of broad- and narrow-spiking neurons.
claims.source: These experiments introduced the concept of broad- and narrow-spiking neurons.
claims.evidence: Directly stated in the introduction as a historical development.

claims.claim: Later experiments in the guinea pig, cat, and the rat helped establish the idea that broad- and narrow-spiking extracellular waveform shapes mostly corresponded to excitatory and inhibitory cells, respectively.
claims.source: Later experiments in the guinea pig (McCormick et al., 1985), cat (Azouz et al., 1997), and the rat (Simons, 1978; Barthó et al., 2004) then helped establish the idea that these broad- and narrow-spiking extracellular waveform shapes mostly corresponded to excitatory and inhibitory cells, respectively.
claims.evidence: Directly stated in the introduction and supported by citations to prior literature.

claims.claim: These results have been used as the basis for identifying cell types in primate recordings.
claims.source: These results have been used as the basis for identifying cell types in primate recordings (Johnston et al., 2009; Merchant et al., 2008; Merchant et al., 2012).
claims.evidence: Directly stated in the introduction and supported by citations to prior literature.

claims.claim: This method of identifying cell types in mammalian cortex in vivo is widely used in neuroscience but it is insufficient to capture the known structural and transcriptomic diversity of cell types in the monkey and the mouse.
claims.source: This method of identifying cell types in mammalian cortex in vivo is widely used in neuroscience but it is insufficient to capture the known structural and transcriptomic diversity of cell types in the monkey and the mouse (Hodge et al., 2019; Krienen et al., 2020).
claims.evidence: Directly stated in the introduction and supported by citations to prior literature.

claims.claim: Recent observations in the monkey defy the simple classification of broad- and narrow-spiking cells as corresponding to excitatory and inhibitory cells, respectively.
claims.source: Furthermore, recent observations in the monkey defy this simple classification of broad- and narrow-spiking cells as corresponding to excitatory and inhibitory cells, respectively.
claims.evidence: Directly stated in the introduction as a challenge to the traditional classification.

claims.claim: Three examples in the primate that have resisted the principle of broad-spiking as excitatory and narrow-spiking as inhibitory are narrow-spiking pyramidal tract neurons in deep layers of M1 (Betz cells), narrow and broad spike widths among excitatory pyramidal tract neurons of premotor cortex, and narrow-spiking excitatory cells in layer III of V1, V2, and MT.
claims.source: Three such examples in the primate that have resisted this principle are narrow-spiking pyramidal tract neurons in deep layers of M1 (Betz cells, Vigneswaran et al., 2011; Soares et al., 2017), narrow and broad spike widths among excitatory pyramidal tract neurons of premotor cortex (Lemon et al., 2021), and narrow-spiking excitatory cells in layer III of V1, V2, and MT (Constantinople et al., 2009; Amatrudo et al., 2012; Onorato et al., 2020; Kelly et al., 2019).
claims.evidence: Directly stated in the introduction and supported by citations to prior literature.

claims.claim: More recent studies have incorporated additional features of EAPs such as trough to peak duration, repolarization time, and triphasic waveform shape.
claims.source: To capture a more representative diversity of cell types in vivo, more recent studies have incorporated additional features of EAPs (beyond AP width) such as trough to peak duration (Ardid et al., 2015), repolarization time (Trainito et al., 2019; Banaie Boroujeni et al., 2021), and triphasic waveform shape (Barry, 2015; Robbins et al., 2013).
claims.evidence: Directly stated in the introduction and supported by citations to prior literature.

claims.claim: User-specified methods are insufficient to distinguish between previously identified cell types.
claims.source: Although these user-specified methods are amenable to human intuition, they are insufficient to distinguish between previously identified cell types (Krimer et al., 2005; Vigneswaran et al., 2011; Merchant et al., 2012).
claims.evidence: Directly stated in the introduction and supported by citations to prior literature.

claims.claim: It is unclear how to choose user-specified features in a principled manner as they are often highly correlated with one another.
claims.source: It is also unclear how to choose these user-specified features in a principled manner (i.e. one set that maximizes explanatory power) as they are often highly correlated with one another.
claims.evidence: Directly stated in the introduction as a limitation of user-specified features.

claims.claim: Different studies choosing between different sets of specified features each yield different inferred cell classes.
claims.source: This results in different studies choosing between different sets of specified features each yielding different inferred cell classes (Trainito et al., 2019; Viskontas et al., 2007; Katai et al., 2010; Sun et al., 2021).
claims.evidence: Directly stated in the introduction and supported by citations to prior literature.

claims.claim: It is difficult to compare putative cell types across literature.
claims.source: Thus, it is difficult to compare putative cell types across literature.
claims.evidence: Directly stated in the introduction as a consequence of different feature choices.

claims.claim: Some studies conclude that there is no single set of specified features that is a reliable differentiator of type.
claims.source: Some studies even conclude that there is no single set of specified features that is a reliable differentiator of type (Weir et al., 2014).
claims.evidence: Directly stated in the introduction and supported by a citation to prior literature.

claims.claim: Non-linear dimensionality reduction methods are designed to find patterns in complex datasets.
claims.source: These issues led us to investigate techniques that do not require feature specification but are designed to find patterns in complex datasets through non-linear dimensionality reduction.
claims.evidence: Directly stated in the introduction as a motivation for using non-linear dimensionality reduction.

claims.claim: Non-linear dimensionality reduction methods have seen usage in diverse neuroscientific contexts such as single-cell transcriptomics, analyzing models of biological neural networks, the identification of behavior, and in electrophysiology.
claims.source: Such methods have seen usage in diverse neuroscientific contexts such as single-cell transcriptomics (Tasic et al., 2018; Becht et al., 2019), in analyzing models of biological neural networks (Maheswaranathan et al., 2019; Kleinman et al., 2019), the identification of behavior (Bala et al., 2020; Hsu and Yttri, 2020; Dolensek et al., 2020), and in electrophysiology (Jia et al., 2019; Gouwens et al., 2020; Klempíř et al., 2020; Markanday et al., 2020; Dimitriadis et al., 2018).
claims.evidence: Directly stated in the introduction and supported by citations to prior literature.

claims.claim: WaveMAP combines Universal Manifold Approximation and Projection (UMAP) with Louvain community detection.
claims.source: Here, in a novel technique that we term WaveMAP, we combine a non-linear dimensionality reduction method (Universal Manifold Approximation and Projection [UMAP], McInnes et al., 2018) with graph community detection (Louvain community detection, (Blondel et al., 2008); we colloquially call 'clustering') to understand the physiological properties, decision-related dynamics, and laminar distribution of candidate cell types during decision-making.
claims.evidence: Directly stated in the introduction and supported by citations to prior literature.

claims.claim: WaveMAP significantly outperformed current approaches without need for user-specification of waveform features like trough to peak duration.
claims.source: We found that WaveMAP significantly outperformed current approaches without need for user-specification of waveform features like trough to peak duration.
claims.evidence: Directly stated in the introduction as a result of the study.

claims.claim: WaveMAP exposed more diversity in extracellular waveform shape than any constructed spike features in isolation or in combination.
claims.source: This data-driven approach exposed more diversity in extracellular waveform shape than any constructed spike features in isolation or in combination.
claims.evidence: Directly stated in the introduction as a result of the study.

claims.claim: Through interpretable machine learning, WaveMAP picks up on nuanced and meaningful biological variability in waveform shape.
claims.source: Using interpretable machine learning, we also show that WaveMAP picks up on nuanced and meaningful biological variability in waveform shape.
claims.evidence: Directly stated in the introduction as a result of the study.

claims.claim: WaveMAP revealed three broad-spiking and five narrow-spiking waveform types.
claims.source: WaveMAP revealed three broad-spiking and five narrow-spiking waveform types that differed significantly in shape, physiological, functional, and laminar distribution properties.
claims.evidence: Directly stated in the introduction as a result of the study.

claims.claim: The three broad-spiking and five narrow-spiking waveform types differed significantly in shape, physiological, functional, and laminar distribution properties.
claims.source: WaveMAP revealed three broad-spiking and five narrow-spiking waveform types that differed significantly in shape, physiological, functional, and laminar distribution properties.
claims.evidence: Directly stated in the introduction as a result of the study.

claims.claim: Most narrow-spiking cells had the high maximum firing rates typically associated with inhibitory neurons.
claims.source: Although most narrow-spiking cells had the high maximum firing rates typically associated with inhibitory neurons, some had firing rates similar to broad-spiking neurons which are typically considered to be excitatory.
claims.evidence: Directly stated in the introduction as a result of the study.

claims.claim: Some narrow-spiking cells had firing rates similar to broad-spiking neurons which are typically considered to be excitatory.
claims.source: Although most narrow-spiking cells had the high maximum firing rates typically associated with inhibitory neurons, some had firing rates similar to broad-spiking neurons which are typically considered to be excitatory.
claims.evidence: Directly stated in the introduction as a result of the study.

claims.claim: The time at which choice selectivity ('discrimination time') emerged for many narrow-spiking cell classes was earlier than broad-spiking neuron classes—except for the narrow-spiking cells that had broad-spiking like maximum firing rates.
claims.source: The time at which choice selectivity ('discrimination time') emerged for many narrow-spiking cell classes was earlier than broad-spiking neuron classes—except for the narrow-spiking cells that had broad-spiking like maximum firing rates.
claims.evidence: Directly stated in the introduction as a result of the study.

claims.claim: Many clusters had distinct laminar distributions that appear layer-dependent in a manner matching certain anatomical cell types.
claims.source: Finally, many clusters had distinct laminar distributions that appear layer-dependent in a manner matching certain anatomical cell types.
claims.evidence: Directly stated in the introduction as a result of the study.

claims.claim: This clustering explains variability in discrimination time over and above previously reported laminar differences.
claims.source: This clustering explains variability in discrimination time over and above previously reported laminar differences (Chandrasekaran et al., 2017).
claims.evidence: Directly stated in the introduction as a result of the study and supported by a citation to prior literature.

claims.claim: The broad-spiking clusters had a trough to peak duration of 0.74 ± 0.24 ms (mean ± S.D.).
claims.source: The broad-spiking clusters had a trough to peak duration of 0.74 ± 0.24 ms (mean ± S.D.) and the narrow-spiking clusters had a trough to peak duration of 0.36 ± 0.07 ms (mean ± S.D.).
claims.evidence: Directly stated in the results section describing the WaveMAP clusters.

claims.claim: The narrow-spiking clusters had a trough to peak duration of 0.36 ± 0.07 ms (mean ± S.D.).
claims.source: The broad-spiking clusters had a trough to peak duration of 0.74 ± 0.24 ms (mean ± S.D.) and the narrow-spiking clusters had a trough to peak duration of 0.36 ± 0.07 ms (mean ± S.D.).
claims.evidence: Directly stated in the results section describing the WaveMAP clusters.

claims.claim: The narrow-spiking set was composed of five clusters with 'narrow-spiking' waveforms (clusters ①, ②, ③, ④, ⑤) and comprised ∼12%, ∼12%, ∼18%, ∼7%, and ∼19% (n = 72, 78, 113, 43, and 116) respectively of the total waveforms, for ∼68% of total waveforms.
claims.source: The narrow-spiking set was composed of five clusters with 'narrow-spiking' waveforms (clusters ①, ②, ③, ④, ⑤) and comprised ∼12%, ∼12%, ∼18%, ∼7%, and ∼19% (n = 72, 78, 113, 43, and 116) respectively of the total waveforms, for ∼68% of total waveforms.
claims.evidence: Directly stated in the results section describing the WaveMAP clusters.

claims.claim: The broad-spiking set was composed of three 'broad-spiking' waveform clusters (⑥, ⑦, and ⑧) comprising ∼13%, ∼5%, and ∼15% (n = 80, 29, and 94) respectively and collectively ∼32% of total waveforms.
claims.source: The broad-spiking set was composed of three 'broad-spiking' waveform clusters (⑥, ⑦, and ⑧) comprising ∼13%, ∼5%, and ∼15% (n = 80, 29, and 94) respectively and collectively ∼32% of total waveforms.
claims.evidence: Directly stated in the results section describing the WaveMAP clusters.

claims.claim: The number of clusters identified by WaveMAP is dependent on the resolution parameter for Louvain clustering.
claims.source: The number of clusters identified by WaveMAP is dependent on the resolution parameter for Louvain clustering.
claims.evidence: Directly stated in the results section describing the parameter selection.

claims.claim: A principled way to choose the resolution parameter is to use the modularity score as the objective function to maximize.
claims.source: A principled way to choose this resolution parameter is to use the modularity score (a measure of how tightly interconnected the members of a cluster are) as the objective function to maximize.
claims.evidence: Directly stated in the results section describing the parameter selection.

claims.claim: A resolution parameter of 1.5 was chosen that maximized modularity score while ensuring that clusters were not overly fractionated (n < 20 within a cluster).
claims.source: We chose a resolution parameter of 1.5 that maximized modularity score while ensuring that we did not overly fractionate the dataset (n < 20 within a cluster; Figure 3A,B, and columns of Figure 3—figure supplement 1A).
claims.evidence: Directly stated in the results section and shown in Figure 3B.

claims.claim: Louvain clustering with a resolution parameter of 1.5 identified eight clusters in total.
claims.source: Louvain clustering with this resolution parameter of 1.5 identified eight clusters in total (Figure 3A).
claims.evidence: Directly stated in the results section and shown in Figure 3A.

claims.claim: Using a slightly higher resolution parameter (2.0) led to seven clusters.
claims.source: Note, using a slightly higher resolution parameter (2.0), a suboptimal solution in terms of modularity, led to seven clusters (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A).
claims.evidence: Directly stated in the results section and shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1A.

claims.claim: The higher resolution parameter merged two of the broad-spiking clusters ⑥ and ⑦ while keeping the rest of the clusters largely intact.
claims.source: Here, we found that the higher resolution parameter merged two of the broad-spiking clusters ⑥ and ⑦ while keeping the rest of the clusters largely intact and more importantly, did not lead to material changes in the conclusions of analyses of physiology, decision-related dynamics, or laminar distribution described below.
claims.evidence: Directly stated in the results section describing the effect of the higher resolution parameter.

claims.claim: An alternative ensembled version of the Louvain clustering algorithm (ensemble clustering for graphs [ECG]) produced a clustering almost exactly the same as the WaveMAP results.
claims.source: Finally, an alternative ensembled version of the Louvain clustering algorithm (ensemble clustering for graphs [ECG] Poulin and Théberge, 2018), which requires setting no resolution parameter, produced a clustering almost exactly the same as our results (Figure 3—figure supplement 1C).
claims.evidence: Directly stated in the results section and shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1C, and supported by a citation to prior literature.

claims.claim: A gradient boosted decision tree classifier trained on the waveform data achieved an average accuracy of 91% across all clusters.
claims.source: After training, the classification was evaluated against the held-out test set (which was never seen in model training/tuning) and the accuracy, averaged over clusters, was 91%.
claims.evidence: Directly stated in the results section describing the classifier performance.

claims.claim: Such successful classification at high levels of accuracy was only possible because there were 'generalizable' clusterings of similar waveform shapes in the high-dimensional space revealed by UMAP.
claims.source: Such successful classification at high levels of accuracy was only possible because there were 'generalizable' clusterings of similar waveform shapes in the high-dimensional space revealed by UMAP.
claims.evidence: Directly stated in the results section as an interpretation of the classifier performance.

claims.claim: Cluster memberships found by WaveMAP are stable with respect to random seed when resolution parameter and n_neighbors parameter are fixed.
claims.source: We find that cluster memberships found by WaveMAP are stable with respect to random seed when resolution parameter and n_neighbors parameter are fixed.
claims.evidence: Directly stated in the results section describing the stability of WaveMAP.

claims.claim: This stability of WaveMAP clusters with respect to random seed is because much of the variability in UMAP layout is the result of the projection process.
claims.source: This stability of WaveMAP clusters with respect to random seed is because much of the variability in UMAP layout is the result of the projection process (Figure 2B–v.a).
claims.evidence: Directly stated in the results section and shown in Figure 2B–v.a.

claims.claim: Louvain clustering operates before the projection step on the high-dimensional graph generated by UMAP which is far less sensitive to the random seed.
claims.source: Louvain clustering operates before this step on the high-dimensional graph generated by UMAP which is far less sensitive to the random seed.
claims.evidence: Directly stated in the results section describing the stability of WaveMAP.

claims.claim: WaveMAP was robust to data subsetting (randomly sampled subsets of the full dataset).
claims.source: We also found that WaveMAP was robust to data subsetting (randomly sampled subsets of the full dataset, see Supplementary Information Tibshirani and Walther, 2005), unlike other clustering approaches (Figure 3—figure supplement 1B, green, Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
claims.evidence: Directly stated in the results section and shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1B and Figure 4—figure supplement 1, and supported by a citation to prior literature.

claims.claim: WaveMAP was consistent in both cluster number and cluster membership across random subsets of the data.
claims.source: WaveMAP was consistent in both cluster number (Figure 3—figure supplement 1B, red) and cluster membership (which waveforms were frequently 'co-members' of the same cluster; Figure 3—figure supplement 1B, green).
claims.evidence: Directly stated in the results section and shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1B.

claims.claim: WaveMAP results were robust to another standard approach to normalizing spike waveforms: normalization to trough depth.
claims.source: Finally, our results were also robust to another standard approach to normalizing spike waveforms: normalization to trough depth. This method exhibited the same stability in cluster number (Figure 3—figure supplement 2C), and also showed no differences in downstream analyses (Figure 3—figure supplement 2D).
claims.evidence: Directly stated in the results section and shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2C and D.

claims.claim: Without amplitude normalization, interesting structure was lost because UMAP likely attempts to explain both waveform amplitude and shape.
claims.source: Without amplitude normalization, interesting structure was lost (Figure 3—figure supplement 2E) because UMAP likely attempts to explain both waveform amplitude and shape (shown as a smooth gradient in the trough to peak height difference Figure 3—figure supplement 2F).
claims.evidence: Directly stated in the results section and shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2E and F.

claims.claim: Common recommendations to apply PCA before non-linear dimensionality reduction were not as important for the waveform dataset, which was fairly low-dimensional (first three PC's explained 94% variance).
claims.source: In addition, common recommendations to apply PCA before non-linear dimensionality reduction were not as important for our waveform dataset, which was fairly low-dimensional (first three PC's explained 94% variance).
claims.evidence: Directly stated in the results section describing the effect of PCA.

claims.claim: Projecting waveforms into a three-dimensional PC-space before WaveMAP produced a clustering very similar to data without this step.
claims.source: Projecting waveforms into a three-dimensional PC-space before WaveMAP produced a clustering very similar to data without this step (Figure 3—figure supplement 3).
claims.evidence: Directly stated in the results section and shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 3.

claims.claim: A Gaussian mixture model (GMM) was applied to the three-dimensional space produced by commonly used waveform features to compare with WaveMAP.
claims.source: To compare how WaveMAP performs relative to traditional clustering methods built on specified features, we applied a Gaussian mixture model (GMM) to the three-dimensional space produced by commonly used waveform features.
claims.evidence: Directly stated in the results section describing the comparison with GMM.

claims.claim: The features chosen for the GMM were action potential (AP) width of the spike, the peak ratio, and the trough to peak duration.
claims.source: In accordance with previous work, the features we chose (Figure 4A) were action potential (AP) width of the spike (width in milliseconds of the full-width half minimum of the depolarization trough Vigneswaran et al., 2011); the peak ratio the ratio of pre-hyperpolarization peak (A1) to the post-hyperpolarization peak (A2) Barry, 2015; and the trough to peak duration (time in ms from the depolarization trough to post-hyperpolarization peak) which is the most common feature used in analyses of extracellular recordings (Snyder et al., 2016; Kaufman et al., 2013; Merchant et al., 2012).
claims.evidence: Directly stated in the results section and shown in Figure 4A, and supported by citations to prior literature.

claims.claim: The GMM identified four waveform clusters that roughly separated into broad-spiking (BS, ∼33%, n = 208), narrow-spiking (NS, ∼43%, n = 269), broad-spiking triphasic (BST, ∼9%, n = 55), and narrow-spiking triphasic (NST, ∼15%, n = 93).
claims.source: The result of the GMM applied to these three measures is shown in Figure 4B. This method identified four waveform clusters that roughly separated into broad-spiking (BS, ∼33%, n = 208), narrow-spiking (NS, ∼43%, n = 269), broad-spiking triphasic (BST, ∼9%, n = 55), and narrow-spiking triphasic (NST, ∼15%, n = 93) (Figure 4B).
claims.evidence: Directly stated in the results section and shown in Figure 4B.

claims.claim: Triphasic waveforms are thought to be neurons with myelinated axons or neurites.
claims.source: Triphasic waveforms, thought to be neurons with myelinated axons or neurites (Barry, 2015; Robbins et al., 2013; Deligkaris et al., 2016; Bakkum et al., 2013; Sun et al., 2021), contain an initial positive spike before the trough and can be identified by large peak ratios (Figure 4A).
claims.evidence: Directly stated in the results section and supported by citations to prior literature.

claims.claim: The GMM clusters are similar to those obtained from other clusterings of EAP's in macaque cortex.
claims.source: These GMM clusters are similar to those obtained from other clusterings of EAP's in macaque cortex (Gur et al., 1999; Trainito et al., 2019).
claims.evidence: Directly stated in the results section and supported by citations to prior literature.

claims.claim: Four clusters were selected by examining the Bayesian information criterion (BIC) statistic as a function of the number of clusters and identifying the cluster number at the elbow.
claims.source: We selected four clusters by examining the Bayesian information citerion (BIC) statistic as a function of the number of clusters and identified the cluster number at the elbow (green chevron in Figure 4C).
claims.evidence: Directly stated in the results section and shown in Figure 4C.

claims.claim: A decision tree classifier trained on the GMM classes achieved an average accuracy of ∼78% across all four classes.
claims.source: After training, the accuracy across all four classes averaged ∼78% with no classification accuracy over 95% and misclassifications between every class (Figure 4D).
claims.evidence: Directly stated in the results section and shown in Figure 4D.

claims.claim: The classifier trained on specified features under-performed the classifier trained on the whole waveform found by WaveMAP.
claims.source: The classifier trained on specified features under-performed the classifier trained on the whole waveform found by WaveMAP.
claims.evidence: Directly stated in the results section comparing the two classifiers.

claims.claim: In WaveMAP, the individual classification accuracy of most classes exceeded 95% with few misclassifications between groups even though there were double the number of clusters.
claims.source: In WaveMAP, the individual classification accuracy of most classes exceeded 95% with few misclassifications between groups even though there were double the number of clusters.
claims.evidence: Directly stated in the results section comparing the two classifiers.

claims.claim: The clusters based on specified features are less differentiable than WaveMAP clusters even when a much lower cluster number is considered.
claims.source: This result suggests that the clusters based on specified features are less differentiable than WaveMAP clusters even when a much lower cluster number is considered.
claims.evidence: Directly stated in the results section as an interpretation of the classifier performance.

claims.claim: The deficit in GMM performance can be understood as an inability of the GMM to fully capture the latent structure of the data.
claims.source: This deficit can be understood as an inability of the GMM to fully capture the latent structure of the data.
claims.evidence: Directly stated in the results section as an interpretation of the GMM performance.

claims.claim: No features in the GMM contain clear clusters and neither do they contain Gaussian distributions which is an assumption of the GMM model.
claims.source: If we examine the gray data point shadows (Figure 4B), no features contain clear clusters and neither do they contain Gaussian distributions which is an assumption of the GMM model.
claims.evidence: Directly stated in the results section and shown in Figure 4B.

claims.claim: Examining the marginal distributions in Figure 4B, none of the features induce a clear separability between the clusters alone or in conjunction.
claims.source: Examining the marginal distributions in Figure 4B, none of the features induce a clear separability between the clusters alone or in conjunction.
claims.evidence: Directly stated in the results section and shown in Figure 4B.

claims.claim: The reproducible clusters found by WaveMAP are linearly inseparable in the feature space of the three GMM features.
claims.source: Furthermore, the reproducible clusters found by WaveMAP are linearly inseparable in the feature space of the three GMM features (Figure 4—figure supplement 2A).
claims.evidence: Directly stated in the results section and shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2A.

claims.claim: Even if the GMM is instantiated with eight clusters, a classifier is still unable to generalize this clustering with even modest accuracy (average of 56% across clusters).
claims.source: Even if the GMM is instantiated with eight clusters (Figure 4—figure supplement 2B), a classifier is still unable to generalize this clustering with even modest accuracy (average of 56% across clusters; Figure 4—figure supplement 2C) even if the waveforms shapes found by the GMM with eight clusters seem somewhat sensible (Figure 4—figure supplement 2D).
claims.evidence: Directly stated in the results section and shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2B, C, and D.

claims.claim: Across all cluster numbers (n_components from 2 to 16), a classifier tuned for the GMM performed more poorly on the GMM labels than a WaveMAP projection with the same number of clusters.
claims.source: In fact, across all cluster numbers (n_components from 2 to 16), a classifier tuned for the GMM performed more poorly on the GMM labels than a WaveMAP projection with the same number of clusters (Figure 4—figure supplement 2E, in red).
claims.evidence: Directly stated in the results section and shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2E.

claims.claim: WaveMAP yielded mappings that were more generalizable than a GMM on features across every number of clusters and both parameters investigated.
claims.source: WaveMAP yielded mappings that were more generalizable than a GMM on features across every number of clusters and both parameters investigated.
claims.evidence: Directly stated in the results section comparing WaveMAP and GMM.

claims.claim: It is a deficit of the GMM on constructed feature-based approach to capture the full diversity of waveforms, especially at high cluster number, and not a peculiarity of the model parameters chosen or number of clusters induced.
claims.source: Thus, it is a deficit of the GMM on constructed feature-based approach to capture the full diversity of waveforms, especially at high cluster number, and not a peculiarity of the model parameters chosen or number of clusters induced.
claims.evidence: Directly stated in the results section as an interpretation of the GMM performance.

claims.claim: WaveMAP implicitly captures each of the specified features (AP width, trough to peak duration, and peak ratio) shown as a smooth gradient of values.
claims.source: We find that WaveMAP implicitly captures each of these specified features shown as a smooth gradient of values.
claims.evidence: Directly stated in the results section describing the representation of specified features in UMAP space.

claims.claim: The gradient between trough to peak duration and AP width points roughly in the same direction so thus both features are highly correlated.
claims.source: Our method also exposes the correlation between certain specified features: the gradient between trough to peak duration and AP width points point roughly in the same direction so thus both features are highly correlated.

results.result: Two macaque monkeys were trained on a red-green decision-making task and 625 neurons were recorded from dorsal premotor cortex (PMd) using single tungsten and U-probe electrodes. Waveforms were filtered, aligned, normalized, and single neurons were isolated using strict criteria including minimal ISI violations.
results.evaluation: Claims C1-C13 describe the experimental setup, behavioral task, recording methods, and preprocessing steps. These are standard methodological claims directly stated in the text and supported by figures showing the task design and recording locations. The methods are clearly described and appropriate for the study.

results.result: WaveMAP is a novel method that combines UMAP (non-linear dimensionality reduction) with Louvain community detection (graph clustering) to identify putative cell types from extracellular waveforms recorded during a decision-making task.
results.evaluation: Claims C14, C15, and C49 describe the core methodological contribution. The method is clearly defined as combining UMAP with Louvain clustering, and the application to PMd recordings is explicitly stated. This is a straightforward methodological description.

results.result: WaveMAP identified eight waveform clusters: five narrow-spiking (68% of neurons) and three broad-spiking (32% of neurons). These clusters recapitulate previously identified narrow- and broad-spiking types while revealing previously unknown diversity within these subtypes.
results.evaluation: Claims C16-C17 and C53-C54 state the main finding of eight clusters with distinct properties. Claims C60-C63 and C67 provide quantitative support showing trough-to-peak durations and cluster proportions. Figure 3A shows clear visual separation of clusters, and the classifier achieved 91% accuracy (C71), indicating robust clustering.

results.result: The number of clusters depends on the Louvain resolution parameter. A resolution of 1.5 was chosen to maximize modularity while maintaining analyzable cluster sizes (n>20). Alternative parameters and methods (resolution 2.0, ECG) produced similar results.
results.evaluation: Claims C64-C70 describe parameter selection and validation. Figure 3B shows modularity optimization, and supplementary figures demonstrate robustness to parameter choices. The approach is principled (maximizing modularity) and validated through alternative methods, supporting the claim that eight clusters is a robust solution.

results.result: WaveMAP clusters are robust and generalizable: a classifier achieved 91% accuracy, clusters are stable across random seeds and data subsets, and results are robust to different normalization methods. Without normalization, structure is lost.
results.evaluation: Claims C71-C81 demonstrate robustness through multiple validation approaches. Figure 3C shows high classification accuracy (91%), and supplementary figures show stability across subsampling and normalization methods. The claim that structure is lost without normalization (C79) is supported by Figure 3—figure supplement 2E-F. These are appropriate validation analyses.

results.result: Traditional GMM clustering on three specified features (AP width, peak ratio, trough-to-peak duration) identified only four clusters with lower classification accuracy (78%) compared to WaveMAP (91%). GMM fails to capture the full diversity of waveforms because features lack clear separability and violate Gaussian assumptions.
results.evaluation: Claims C82-C99 compare WaveMAP to traditional methods. Figure 4 shows GMM results with four clusters and lower classifier accuracy. The claims about poor separability (C93-C94) and linear inseparability (C95) are supported by Figure 4B and supplementary figures. The comparison demonstrates WaveMAP's superiority across multiple cluster numbers (C97, Figure 4—figure supplement 2E).

results.result: WaveMAP implicitly captures specified features (AP width, trough-to-peak, peak ratio) as smooth gradients in UMAP space. The correlation between features exposes their redundancy. WaveMAP also identifies intermediate clusters that would be split by GMM despite having distinct waveform shapes.
results.evaluation: Claims C100-C107 describe how WaveMAP relates to traditional features. Figure 5—figure supplement 1 shows features as gradients in UMAP space, supporting C100-C101. The claim about cluster ② being split by GMM (C106-C107) is supported by Figure 4E. This demonstrates that WaveMAP captures and extends beyond traditional features.

results.result: Inverse UMAP transform and SHAP analysis reveal that WaveMAP uses biologically meaningful features. UMAP-1 captures repolarization rate (post-hyperpolarization sharpness) and UMAP-2 captures post-hyperpolarization width, suggesting these are independent factors related to potassium channel dynamics.
results.evaluation: Claims C108-C118 describe interpretable machine learning results. Figure 5A shows inverse transform results with smooth transitions in waveform shape along UMAP dimensions. The biological interpretation linking to K+ channels (C117) is supported by citation. This demonstrates that WaveMAP captures biologically meaningful variation, though the K+ channel interpretation is somewhat speculative.

results.result: SHAP analysis identifies which waveform time points are most informative for cluster classification. Key regions include 0.5-0.65 ms (post-hyperpolarization peak), 0.3-0.4 ms (pre-hyperpolarization peak), and 0.6 ms (inflection point), recapitulating known features. Novel regions at 1.1 and 1.27 ms suggest using >1.0 ms of waveform is important.
results.evaluation: Claims C119-C132 describe SHAP analysis results. Figure 5B-C shows SHAP values identifying important time points. The claim that known features are recapitulated (C126-C128) is supported by citations. The novel finding about later time points (C129-C130) is data-driven. This provides interpretability and suggests methodological improvements for future studies.

results.result: WaveMAP clusters exhibit distinct baseline firing rates. Broad-spiking clusters have significantly lower baseline FR than narrow-spiking clusters (p=0.0028). However, there is heterogeneity within both groups, with some narrow-spiking clusters (②, ③, ④) having low baseline FR similar to broad-spiking neurons.
results.evaluation: Claims C18-C19 and C133-C142 describe baseline FR differences. Figure 6C shows significant differences between broad and narrow groups, and within narrow-spiking clusters. Statistical tests are appropriate (Mann-Whitney U, FDR adjusted). The finding of heterogeneity within narrow-spiking neurons (C140-C142) is well-supported and challenges simple excitatory/inhibitory classification.

results.result: Maximum firing rates differ significantly between broad- and narrow-spiking clusters (p=1.60e-5). Broad-spiking clusters are homogeneous with low max FR (~24 spikes/s). Narrow-spiking clusters show heterogeneity: three clusters (①, ③, ⑤) have high max FR (~33 spikes/s) while two (②, ④) have low max FR (~23 spikes/s) comparable to broad-spiking.
results.evaluation: Claims C143-C147 describe max FR differences. Figure 6D shows clear differences with appropriate statistics. The heterogeneity within narrow-spiking neurons is striking and well-documented. This finding challenges the assumption that all narrow-spiking neurons are inhibitory with high firing rates.

results.result: Firing rate range (max FR - baseline FR) differs significantly between broad- and narrow-spiking clusters (p=0.0002). Broad-spiking clusters show uniform FR range (~10.8 spikes/s). Narrow-spiking clusters show heterogeneity: ①, ③, ⑤ have large FR range (~20 spikes/s) while ②, ④ have smaller range (~13 spikes/s).
results.evaluation: Claims C148-C153 describe FR range differences. Figure 6E shows the pattern parallels max FR results. The consistency across multiple FR measures (baseline, max, range) strengthens the conclusion that narrow-spiking neurons are physiologically heterogeneous. Statistics are appropriate.

results.result: WaveMAP produces better clustering of physiological properties than GMM. Effect sizes for WaveMAP vs GMM are larger for baseline FR (0.070 vs 0.013), max FR (0.035 vs 0.011), and FR range (0.055 vs 0.034). GMM loses significant differences despite comparing fewer groups.
results.evaluation: Claims C154-C158 compare WaveMAP and GMM for physiological clustering. Effect sizes (Cohen's f²) quantitatively demonstrate WaveMAP's superiority. Figure 6—figure supplement 1 shows GMM results with fewer significant differences. This validates that WaveMAP identifies biologically meaningful clusters beyond just waveform shape.

results.result: WaveMAP clusters show distinct choice-related dynamics. The rate of rise of choice-selective signals as a function of coherence (coherence slope) varies across clusters. Broad-spiking clusters show modest coherence dependence. Narrow-spiking clusters ① and ⑤ show strong coherence dependence, while ②, ③, ④ are similar to broad-spiking.
results.evaluation: Claims C159-C171 describe functional differences during decision-making. Figure 7A-E shows choice-selective signals and coherence slopes. The heterogeneity within narrow-spiking neurons parallels physiological findings. Methods for calculating rate of rise (C166) and coherence slope (C169) are clearly described. This demonstrates functional relevance of WaveMAP clusters.

results.result: Discrimination time (when choice selectivity emerges) differs across clusters. Broad-spiking clusters have significantly later discrimination times (255±94 ms) than narrow-spiking (224±89 ms, p<0.005). Clusters ① and ⑤ with highest max FR and strongest coherence modulation have fastest discrimination times (~200 ms).
results.evaluation: Claims C172-C179 describe discrimination time differences. Figure 7F shows clear differences with appropriate statistics. The method (bootstrap test, C173) is appropriate. The finding that not all narrow-spiking neurons are faster (C177) and that ① and ⑤ are fastest (C178) is consistent with physiological and choice dynamics results, providing converging evidence.

results.result: Broad-spiking clusters (⑥, ⑦, ⑧) are centered in middle-to-deep layers with broad distributions and no significant laminar differences between them. Overall narrow- and broad-spiking populations do not differ significantly in distribution (p=0.24).
results.evaluation: Claims C180-C190 describe laminar distributions of broad-spiking clusters. Figure 8A shows distributions. The caveat about alignment errors (C184-C185) is appropriate and the focus on relative comparisons (C186-C187) is justified. The lack of difference between overall narrow/broad populations (C188) is interesting given other differences.

results.result: Narrow-spiking clusters show distinct laminar distributions. Cluster ① has broad distribution, ② is localized at 1.1±0.33 mm, ③ is superficial at 1.0±0.6 mm, ④ is deep (1.70±0.44 mm) with triphasic waveforms suggesting myelinated pyramidal cells, and ⑤ has broad distribution at 1.3±0.65 mm.
results.evaluation: Claims C191-C198 describe narrow-spiking laminar distributions. Figure 8B shows distinct distributions with significant statistical differences. The interpretation of ④ as myelinated pyramidal cells (C197) is supported by citations and waveform shape. The diversity of laminar distributions suggests different cell types.

results.result: GMM clusters show no significant laminar differences (all p>0.2 except BS vs BST p=0.067) and exhibit broad distributions across cortex, inconsistent with known cell type distributions from histology.
results.evaluation: Claims C199-C201 show GMM fails to capture laminar organization. Figure 8C shows broad, overlapping distributions. The comparison to WaveMAP demonstrates another dimension where WaveMAP outperforms traditional methods. The claim about inconsistency with histology (C201) sets up the next analysis.

results.result: Immunohistochemistry shows CB+ and CR+ interneurons have similar restricted superficial distributions most closely resembling WaveMAP cluster ③. CB+ and CR+ cells have similar physiological properties and spike shapes.
results.evaluation: Claims C202-C208 compare WaveMAP to anatomical data. Figure 9C-D shows CB+ and CR+ distributions matching cluster ③. The stereological counting method (C205) is appropriate. The claim about similar physiology (C207) is supported by citation. This provides anatomical validation for at least one WaveMAP cluster.

results.result: WaveMAP cluster ① has laminar properties consistent with PV+ neurons (concentrated superficially, proliferating to middle layers). Both have low baseline FR, early stimulus responses, and robust FR modulation. Cluster ⑤ may also correspond to PV+ cells.
results.evaluation: Claims C209-C212 link cluster ① to PV+ neurons. Figure 9B and E show matching laminar distributions. The physiological similarities (C211) are supported by data and citations. The speculation about ⑤ (C212) is appropriately tentative. This provides strong evidence that ① corresponds to PV+ interneurons.

results.result: IHC results suggest narrow-spiking WaveMAP clusters potentially map onto different inhibitory types (PV+, CR+, CB+).
results.evaluation: Claim C213 summarizes the IHC findings. The evidence from C206-C212 supports this conclusion, though the mapping is not complete (only 3 of 5 narrow-spiking clusters are discussed). The use of 'potentially' is appropriate given the indirect nature of the comparison.

results.result: WaveMAP clusters explain more variance in discrimination time (6.6%) than cortical depth alone (1.7%) or GMM clusters (3.3%). Combined with depth, WaveMAP explains 7.3% vs GMM's 4.6%. This demonstrates WaveMAP clusters are not artifacts of layer-dependent inputs and both cell type and layer contribute to decision-related responses.
results.evaluation: Claims C214-C226 show WaveMAP explains functional heterogeneity better than alternatives. The regression analysis is appropriate and variance explained (R²) values are clearly reported. The comparison to prior work (C216-C217) provides context. This demonstrates that WaveMAP clusters have functional relevance beyond anatomical organization.

results.result: WaveMAP significantly outperforms current approaches without requiring user-specified features, exposes more diversity than specified features, and provides a more nuanced understanding of cell type dynamics in cortical circuits.
results.evaluation: Claims C21-C22 and C50-C52 are high-level conclusions. These are supported by the cumulative evidence: WaveMAP finds 8 clusters vs GMM's 4 (C16, C84), achieves higher classification accuracy (91% vs 78%, C71, C88), better captures physiological properties (C158), functional properties (C218-C221), and laminar organization (C199-C200). The conclusion is well-supported.

results.result: Most narrow-spiking cells have high max FR typical of inhibitory neurons, but some have FR similar to broad-spiking (excitatory) neurons. Discrimination time for many narrow-spiking classes is earlier than broad-spiking—except for narrow-spiking cells with broad-spiking-like max FR. Clustering explains discrimination time variability beyond laminar differences.
results.evaluation: Claims C55-C59 are summary statements supported by detailed results in C146-C147 (max FR heterogeneity), C174-C175 (discrimination time), and C217-C219 (variance explained). These integrate multiple findings into coherent conclusions about narrow-spiking heterogeneity. Well-supported by converging evidence.

results.result: Background and motivation: Cortical circuits contain many cell types that coordinate to produce behavior. Current methods using specified waveform features capture limited variation and are insufficient to distinguish cell types. Different studies use different features, making cross-study comparisons difficult. Non-linear dimensionality reduction offers an alternative approach.
results.evaluation: Claims C23-C48 provide background and motivation. These are knowledge claims supported by extensive citations to prior literature. The characterization of current methods' limitations (C24-C25, C42-C46) is well-documented in cited work. This establishes the need for WaveMAP.
